      <content name="title"><span class="qt3">Kidney</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hypernephroma</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt3">Renal</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>You have two <span class="qt3">kidneys</span>. They are fist-sized organs on either side of your backbone above your waist. The tubes inside filter and clean your blood, taking out waste products and making urine.  <span class="qt3">Kidney</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> forms in the lining of tiny tubes inside your <span class="qt3">kidneys</span>. </p><p><span class="qt3">Kidney</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> becomes more likely as you age. Risk factors include smoking, having certain genetic conditions, and misusing pain medicines for a long time.</p><p>You may have no symptoms at first. They may appear as the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> grows. See your health care provider if you notice:</p><ul><li>Blood in your urine</li><li>A lump in your abdomen</li><li>Weight loss for no reason</li><li>Pain in your side that does not go away</li><li>Loss of appetite</li></ul><p>Tests to diagnose <span class="qt3">kidney</span> <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> include blood, urine, and imaging tests. You may also have a biopsy.</p><p>Treatment depends on your age, your overall health and how advanced the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> is. It might include surgery, chemotherapy, or radiation, biologic, or targeted therapies.  Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> with less harm to normal <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/uterinefibroids.html">
      <content name="title">Uterine Fibroids</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Fibroids</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Uterine Leiomyomata</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are uterine fibroids?<p>Uterine fibroids are the most common noncancerous (benign) <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">tumors</span></span> in women of childbearing age. You may have uterine fibroids and not even know it since they often don't cause any symptoms. Fibroids are made of muscle <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span> and other tissues that grow in and around the wall of the uterus, or womb. They can vary in number and size and grow as one <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">tumor</span></span> or in clusters.</p><p>Many women with fibroids can get pregnant with no problems. However, some uterine fibroids could cause infertility (not being able to get pregnant), pregnancy loss, or problems with fetal development or delivery.</p>Who is more likely to get uterine fibroids?<p>If you're a female and the age when you're usually able to get pregnant and give birth, you could develop fibroids. Some factors may increase your risk of having uterine fibroids. These can include:</p><ul><li>Age. Women who are older have a higher risk.</li><li>Race/ethnicity. Black/African American women often have fibroids at a younger age. They're also more likely to have larger fibroids with worse symptoms.</li><li>Family history. If your mother or sister had uterine fibroids.</li><li>Other factors. If you started your period before age 10 or have never been pregnant.</li><li>Certain medical conditions. These include obesity or vitamin D deficiency.</li></ul><p>Your risk of getting uterine fibroids lowers with each pregnancy and with long-term use of birth control pills or shots.</p>What causes uterine fibroids?<p>No one knows what causes uterine fibroids. A few things that might play a part in getting uterine fibroids include genetics and growth hormones. Also, other hormones like estrogen and progesterone seem to help fibroids grow. These hormones cause the tissue lining inside the uterus to thicken during each menstrual cycle to prepare for pregnancy.</p>What are the symptoms of uterine fibroids?<p>Many women with fibroids have no symptoms. If you do, the type of symptoms may be due to location, size, and number of fibroids. Symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Heavy or painful periods or bleeding between periods</li><li>Feeling "full" in the lower abdomen (belly)</li><li>Urinating (peeing) often</li><li>Pain during sex</li><li>Lower back pain</li><li>Problems getting pregnant, multiple miscarriages, or early labor while pregnant</li></ul>How are uterine fibroids diagnosed?<p>You may not know that you have uterine fibroids unless you have symptoms. Or your health care provider may find the fibroids during a pelvic exam, or with imaging tests.</p><p>Uterine fibroids might be very small, or in extreme cases, they may grow large enough to make it appear like a pregnancy.</p>What are the treatments for uterine fibroids?<p>If you have no symptoms, you may not even need treatment. If you have symptoms, the treatment for uterine fibroids depends on many factors. These can include:</p><ul><li>Your symptoms.</li><li>Your age. Sometimes fibroids shrink during and after menopause due to a drop in hormone levels.</li><li>The location, type, and size of fibroids.</li><li>If you are pregnant or want to get pregnant in the future.</li></ul><p>Treatment may include medicines that can slow or stop fibroid growth. Surgery, such as a hysterectomy (removal of the uterus), may be considered if you are near or past menopause, your fibroids are very large or cause heavy bleeding.</p><p>If you are having trouble getting pregnant, your provider may discuss infertility treatments. They may also recommend an emotional support group if you have chronic symptoms or difficulties getting pregnant or maintaining a pregnancy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Child Health and Human Development</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/bladdercancer.html">
      <content name="title">Bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Urinary Bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>The bladder is a hollow organ in your lower abdomen that stores urine. Bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> occurs in the lining of the bladder. It is the sixth most common type of <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> in the United States.</p><p>Symptoms include:</p><ul><li>Blood in your urine</li><li>A frequent urge to urinate</li><li>Pain when you urinate</li><li>Low back pain</li></ul><p>Risk factors for developing bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> include smoking and exposure to certain chemicals in the workplace.  People with a family history of bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> or who are older, White, or male have a higher risk.</p><p>Treatments for bladder <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and biologic therapy. Biologic therapy boosts your body's own ability to fight <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/ureteraldisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ureteral Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ureteral <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt3">kidneys</span> make urine by filtering wastes and extra water from your blood.  The urine travels from the <span class="qt3">kidneys</span> to the bladder in two thin tubes called ureters.</p><p>The ureters are about 8 to 10 inches long. Muscles in the ureter walls tighten and relax to force urine down and away from the <span class="qt3">kidneys</span>. Small amounts of urine flow from the ureters into the bladder about every 10 to 15 seconds.</p><p>Sometimes the ureters can become blocked or injured. This can block the flow of urine to the bladder. If urine stands still or backs up the ureter, you may get a urinary tract infection.</p><p>Doctors diagnose problems with the ureters using different tests. These include urine tests, x-rays, and examination of the ureter with a scope called a cystoscope. Treatment depends on the cause of the problem. It may include medicines and, in severe cases, surgery.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and <span class="qt3">Kidney</span> Diseases</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/nuclearscans.html">
      <content name="title">Nuclear Scans</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PET Scans</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Radionuclide Scans</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Radioisotope scans</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a nuclear scan?<p>A nuclear scan is a type of medical imaging test that uses a small amount of radioactive material, called a radiotracer. This scan shows how organs and tissues are working, not just what they look like.</p><p>After the radiotracer is given, a special camera detects the radiation coming from inside the body. This allows your health care provider to see organ function, blood flow, or tissue activity, which can help diagnose conditions and check how well treatment is working.</p>Who needs a nuclear scan?<p>Nuclear scans may be used to find disease, target certain <span class="qt4"><span class="qt5">cells</span></span>, and monitor response to treatment. They are commonly used to:</p><ul><li>Check how organs such as the heart, lungs, or <span class="qt3">kidneys</span> are working</li><li>Find disease early, sometimes before changes can be seen on other imaging tests</li><li>Perform bone scans</li><li>Evaluate the thyroid</li><li>Check how well <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">cancer</span></span> treatment is working</li></ul>How do you prepare for a nuclear scan?<p>Before the scan, you will receive a small amount of radiotracer. This may be given as:</p><ul><li>An injection</li><li>A pill or liquid to swallow</li><li>A gas to inhale</li></ul><p>The radiotracer travels to the part of the body being examined. How much of the tracer is absorbed can help show how well an organ or tissue is functioning.</p><p>Always tell your provider if you are pregnant, think you may be pregnant, or are breastfeeding.</p>How is a nuclear scan done?<p>You may be asked to change clothes and remove jewelry or other items that could interfere with the scan. Ask your provider if there are any special instructions before your scan.</p><p>Depending on the type of nuclear scan, you may:</p><ul><li>Lie on a table</li><li>Sit in a chair</li><li>Stand</li><li>Walk on a treadmill or ride a stationary bike (for some heart scans)</li></ul><p>You will be asked to stay as still as possible, unless movement is part of the test.</p><p>A special imaging device, such as a gamma camera, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) scanner, or positron emission tomography (PET) scanner, detects radiation from the tracer and creates images.</p><p>The length of the scan depends on the type of test and the area being examined. Some scans take only minutes. Others may include waiting periods or require you to return later the same day or over several days.</p>What should you expect after a nuclear scan?<p>Most people can return to normal activities right away. Drinking fluids may help your body clear the radiotracer.</p><p>A specialist called a radiologist reviews the images and shares the results with your provider.</p></content>
